Wednesday night through Friday: The Thanksgiving period will be
quite active across the Inland Northwest as back-to-back 
weather systems move through the region. The first comes tonight
through Thursday as a surface low approaches the British 
Columbia coast, with the warm front spreading northward through 
the region tonight into Thursday morning followed by a trailing 
cold front late Thursday morning through the afternoon. As the 
warm front lifts across the Inland Northwest, it will be 
accompanied by a rather juicy moisture plume (precipitable water
values greater than 200% of normal) embedded within the 
southwesterly flow. Enhanced by a strong upper-level jet, 
widespread precipitation is expected across the Inland 
Northwest. Snow levels will rise above 5000-6000 feet through 
the day today, with snow primarily influencing Washington Pass 
and Sherman Pass along SR 20. Moderate to heavy snow is expected
over Washington Pass with 10th to 90th percentile snowfall 
amounts between 8 and 16 inches through Thursday night. A Winter
Storm Warning is currently in effect from 7 PM Wednesday 
through 4 AM Friday for elevations about 5000 feet for western 
Okanogan County. Travel over Washington Pass will be difficult 
tonight through Thursday. Consider alternate routes if traveling
across Washington during this time. For Sherman Pass, snow 
amounts up to 3 inches will result in slick travel. The upper 
Methow Valley around Mazama may experience heavy, wet snow as 
models projected maximum wet bulb temperatures in the 0-4 km 
layer to be below freezing during the onset of precipitation 
before warming above freezing late Thursday morning. 

A trailing cold front moves eastward late Thursday morning 
through the afternoon, shifting precipitation into far eastern 
Washington and north Idaho while bringing an end to 
precipitation in central Washington. 25th to 75th percentile 
precipitation amounts indicates 0.10 to 0.50 inches in the 
Columbia Basin and L-C Valley, 0.40 to 0.1 inch across the 
Okanogan Valley, far eastern Washington, and the north Idaho 
valleys, 0.80 to 1.2 inch in the Idaho Panhandle mountains, and 
1.50 to 3 inches in the Cascades. These amounts may result in 
rises on smaller creeks and streams on the Palouse and in the 
lee of the Blue Mountains, but no flooding is currently 
expected. Winds will also increase with this front with 
southwest wind gusts up to 35 mph across the Columbia Basin, 
Palouse, and Spokane area. Orographic showers persist along the 
Cascades and the Idaho Panhandle behind the cold front, which 
will bring additional high level snow.

For Friday, models have come into better agreement with a weak 
low and compact shortwave to move into the Pacific Northwest, 
though there still remains differences on the exact path and 
strength. Ensembles generally have the low’s track along the 
Washington/Oregon coast and the bulk of precipitation across the
southern half of Washington and the Idaho Panhandle. A track 
farther north would shift precipitation north, while a track 
farther south would push it south. Due to this, there is a 
dramatic spread in 10th to 90th percentile precipitation amounts
with the 10th percentile amounts near 0 across the entire 
Inland Northwest outside of the southern Idaho Panhandle and far
southeast Washington where 10th percentile amounts are 0.10 to 
0.20 between Pullman and Lewiston and around 0.40 inches over 
the Camas Prairie. Looking at 90th percentile amounts increase 
to 0.50 to 1.40 inches across the entirety of the southern half 
of eastern Washington and the Idaho Panhandle and 0.05 to 0.20 
inches across the far northeast Washington and far north Idaho. 
Snow levels would lower enough to support snow across the 
mountains. 

Saturday through Tuesday: Models are in agreement with a brief 
ridge to move over the Inland Northwest on Saturday with a brief
lull in precipitation. Active weather returns for early next 
week with ensembles in agreement for additional systems to move 
into the Pacific Northwest. Right now the forecast leans toward 
additional mountain snow and lowland rain. /vmt
